Yes, it's the reverse of a warning. Jehu says, “…do not let anyone escape from the city to go and tell it in Jezreel.” (2 Kings 9:15) So no runner leaves to spread the news. He wants to be the first one through the door.
That's him. The text says Ahaziah king of Judah had gone down to see Joram (2 Kings 9:16). Joram is laid up in Jezreel, so Ahaziah is basically visiting a patient. Jehu is about to crash that visit.

Good guess on the name, but it's not the visitor here. In this passage, Jehoshaphat is Jehu's father: “Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi” (2 Kings 9:14). The king who came down to see Joram is Ahaziah king of Judah (2 Kings 9:16). Easy to mix up when the names keep stacking like cookies on a rack.

Ben-hadad is a name for a king of Aram, but he isn't in this passage. The king of Aram here is Hazael, the one Joram was fighting (2 Kings 9:15). The king who came to visit Joram in Jezreel is Ahaziah of Judah (2 Kings 9:16). That's a different crown from a different country.

Yes, that's the question. Joram tells his men, “Send him out to meet them and ask, ‘Have you come in peace?’” (2 Kings 9:17) Simple question, but it's about to get a very strange answer. I think Joram expected a plain yes or no.
That's a smart thing to ask, but it's not what Joram says. He wants the rider to ask, “Have you come in peace?” (2 Kings 9:17) Nothing about names. The rider has one question to carry.

Counting heads is a fair idea, but Joram doesn't ask for it. The rider is sent to ask, “Have you come in peace?” (2 Kings 9:17) The watchman had only said he saw a company of troops. The king's question is about peace.

That's it. Jehu says, “What do you know about peace?” and then, “Fall in behind me.” (2 Kings 9:18) The messenger came to ask a question and got drafted. Not a bad day for the troops, but Joram's rider didn't see that coming.

That would be the usual plan, but it's not what happens. Jehu says, “Fall in behind me.” (2 Kings 9:18) The watchman then reports, “The messenger reached them, but he is not coming back.” (2 Kings 9:18) So the king gets no answer from his rider.
Waiting sounds calm, and Jehu isn't in a calm mood. He tells the horseman, “Fall in behind me.” (2 Kings 9:18) That means the rider joins the line moving toward Jezreel. No roadside sitting.

Yep. The watchman says the charioteer “is driving like Jehu son of Nimshi” (2 Kings 9:20). He recognizes the driving style from way up on that tower. I'd be nervous if somebody recognized my driving from that far away.
It's actually true. The watchman reports, “And the charioteer is driving like Jehu son of Nimshi” (2 Kings 9:20). He doesn't say it's a stranger. He names Jehu from the tower.

explanations.answer: Rides out in his own chariot
explanations.explanation: Right. Joram shouts, “Harness!” and they harness his chariot (2 Kings 9:21). Then Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah set out, each in his own chariot. Two riders went out and didn't come back, so the king goes himself.

I get the thought, but the text doesn't say that. After the second horseman, Joram shouts, “Harness!” (2 Kings 9:21). Then he and Ahaziah set out, each in his own chariot. The king goes himself this time.

Shutting the gates is something a king might do, but the text doesn't mention it. What it says is that Joram shouts, “Harness!” and they harness his chariot (2 Kings 9:21). Then he and Ahaziah ride out to meet Jehu.

That's it. Jehu says, “How can there be peace… as long as the idolatry and witchcraft of your mother Jezebel abound?” (2 Kings 9:22) Jezebel is Joram's mother. So Joram asks a yes or no question and gets a no, with a reason.

Joram does have the king of Judah riding beside him, but that isn't Jehu's answer. He says, “How can there be peace… as long as the idolatry and witchcraft of your mother Jezebel abound?” (2 Kings 9:22) Jehu points at Jezebel, Joram's mother.

explanations.answer: The war with Hazael of Aram
explanations.explanation: The war with Hazael is in this story, since Joram was wounded in it (2 Kings 9:15). But it's not what Jehu names. He says, “How can there be peace… as long as the idolatry and witchcraft of your mother Jezebel abound?” (2 Kings 9:22) His answer is about Jezebel.

Yes, he flees. Joram turns around and flees, calling out to Ahaziah, “Treachery, Ahaziah!” (2 Kings 9:23) One look at Jehu and he heads the other way. I think he knew right then this was no friendly visit.
Nope, no attack from Joram. The text says he “turned around and fled” (2 Kings 9:23). He calls out a warning to Ahaziah as he goes. He's running, not fighting.
Surrender would mean staying put, and Joram doesn't. He turns around and flees, calling out, “Treachery, Ahaziah!” (2 Kings 9:23) He's trying to get away.

That's a natural guess, but Jehu doesn't say it. He tells Bidkar, “Pick him up and throw him into the field of Naboth the Jezreelite.” (2 Kings 9:25) The body goes to that field. Jehu says it's according to the word of the LORD (2 Kings 9:26).

A burial with his fathers is what happens to Ahaziah later (2 Kings 9:28). For Joram, Jehu says, “Pick him up and throw him into the field of Naboth the Jezreelite.” (2 Kings 9:25) That's a very different ending. Jehu says it's according to the word of the LORD (2 Kings 9:26).

Yes. Jehu says, “Now then, according to the word of the LORD, pick him up and throw him on the plot of ground.” (2 Kings 9:26) He points back to what the LORD declared about the blood of Naboth and his sons. This part of the story is heavy, and Jehu ties it to what the LORD had said.

It's true, friend. Jehu says, “Now then, according to the word of the LORD, pick him up and throw him on the plot of ground.” (2 Kings 9:26) He is pointing back to the LORD's word about repaying on that plot of ground. It's a hard part, but he names the word of the LORD himself.
That's what he shouts. Jehu pursues Ahaziah, “shouting, ‘Shoot him too!’” (2 Kings 9:27) The word too tells you the plan didn't stop with Joram. Ahaziah was right to do his math fast.
Jehu doesn't say that. He chases Ahaziah, shouting, “Shoot him too!” (2 Kings 9:27) There was no letting go on that road.
That would be a gentler chase, but the text doesn't say that. Jehu shouts, “Shoot him too!” (2 Kings 9:27) That's an order, not a rescue. The shot happens on the Ascent of Gur.

Right. His servants carried him by chariot to Jerusalem and buried him with his fathers in his tomb in the City of David (2 Kings 9:28). Ahaziah was king of Judah, so that's home. His servants got him there.

Samaria doesn't come up here. The text says his servants carried him to Jerusalem (2 Kings 9:28). He is buried with his fathers in his tomb in the City of David. That's the king of Judah's family tomb.
Bethel isn't in this part of the story. His servants carried Ahaziah by chariot to Jerusalem (2 Kings 9:28). They buried him with his fathers in the City of David. That's where a king of Judah goes.

explanations.answer: Paints her eyes and watches from a window
explanations.explanation: Yes. The text says Jezebel “painted her eyes, adorned her head, and looked down from a window.” (2 Kings 9:30) She isn't hiding. I think she wanted to be seen.

explanations.answer: Hides in a room deep in the palace
explanations.explanation: That's what many people would do, but the text says something else. Jezebel “painted her eyes, adorned her head, and looked down from a window.” (2 Kings 9:30) She's up where Jehu can see her.

explanations.answer: Slips out of the city before dark
explanations.explanation: No sneaking out for her. The text says she “painted her eyes, adorned her head, and looked down from a window.” (2 Kings 9:30) She stays right where Jehu can find her.
That's right. Jehu looks up at the window and calls out, “Who is on my side? Who?” (2 Kings 9:32) He says it twice, like a man who needs an answer now. And two or three eunuchs look down.

No priest in this line. Jehu says to bury her, “for she was the daughter of a king.” (2 Kings 9:34) That's the reason he gives.
